# Ādiccupaṭṭhānajātaka (Ja 175)

**ID:** Ja 175
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Ādiccupaṭṭhānajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ādiccupaṭṭhānajātaka* (Ja 175) is a canonical birth story found in the Jātaka collection. As recorded in the canonical-commentarial framing, the story was told by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana regarding a rogue or hypocritical monk (*kuhaka*), with the opening verse beginning *Sabbesu kira bhūtesu* [Fausböll 1879]. In the past story set during the reign of Brahmadatta in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in Kāsi, studied at Takkasilā, and went forth as an ascetic leader (*gaṇasatthā*) [Fausböll 1879]. The narrative centers on a mischievous monkey who hypocritically mimics religious devotions by posturing as if venerating the sun [Revire 2016; Fausböll 1879]. In the *samodhāna*, the Buddha reveals that the deceitful monkey was reborn as the rogue monk, the ascetic disciples were the Buddhist community, and the ascetic master was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1879].

Scholars note that the text functions as Buddhist satire directed against contemporary solar cults and ritual sun-worship (*ādiccupaṭṭhāna*), a practice condemned as wrong livelihood in the *Brahmajālasutta* of the *Dīgha Nikāya* and subjected to mockery in this Jātaka [Dayal 1932; Revire 2016].

**Sources**

- [Dayal 1932] Har Dayal, The Bodhisattva Doctrine in Buddhist Sanskrit Literature (1932) — Mentions the ridicule of sun-worship in the Ādiccupaṭṭhānajātaka in the context of Indian solar cults.
- [Revire 2016] Nicolas Revire, Enthroned Buddha in Majesty. An Iconological Study (2016) — Analyzes the text's mockery of sun worship in relation to the Brahmajālasutta and the story of the mischievous monkey.
- [Fausböll 1879] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its commentary, Vol. 2 (1879) — Provides the Pali text, verse incipit, Jetavana setting, past story details, and the identification of characters.
